video_title: SpaceX, Palantir, Anduril & Onodrim | The Return of Conglomerates
gist: 137 Ventures' Christian Garrett argues newly public SpaceX (Q3: ~160% growth, $4.4B net income, ~20-30x 2027 EBITDA at ~$2T) is becoming a vertically integrated hyperscaler with sub-12-month compute paybacks while Starship remains underpriced. He lays out a 'return of the conglomerate' thesis (Anduril's Lattice flywheel, dual-use Palantir/SpaceX) and explains his co-founded European platform (transcribed 'Onadrim') that consolidates the overlooked defense supplier layer, since production rather than spending is the bottleneck.

insights.claim: 137 Ventures has held SpaceX for 16 years and it is the firm's largest position; Garrett calls it the company he is most excited about and 'the most important company in the world'.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Long-tenured insider remains maximally bullish post-IPO; signals early holders are not rushing to exit.
insights.quote: it's still the company we are most excited about. I think the most important company in the world.

insights.claim: SpaceX's Q3 showed top-line growth of roughly 160%, $4.4 billion of net income and roughly $8.8-10 billion of EBITDA.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Hard datapoints on newly public SpaceX's scale and profitability; benchmark for valuation work.
insights.quote: they grew topline like 160% they you know posted $4.4 billion in net income

insights.claim: SpaceX is trading at roughly 20-30x consensus EBITDA for 2027 as a ~$2 trillion company dominant in multiple critical industries, which Garrett frames as reasonable given its positioning.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Insider valuation frame: 20-30x out-year EBITDA for a ~$2T multi-industry monopoly-like asset.
insights.quote: it's a business that's trading anywhere from 20 to 30 times 207 for a two trillion dollar company

insights.claim: The underappreciated SpaceX story is that it is becoming a true hyperscaler, building software and services around its compute stack and outrunning the neocloud market.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Value SpaceX's AI/compute segment against hyperscalers (AWS, Google Cloud) rather than neoclouds; negative read-across for standalone neoclouds.
insights.quote: they're clearly like running leaps and bounds around the neocloud market and stepping into being a true hyperscaler.

insights.claim: SpaceX reiterated on earnings calls that its compute buildout achieves sub-12-month payback periods, which Garrett reads as a strong demand signal given supply currently cannot meet demand.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Sub-12-month payback is the key metric de-risking AI capex; watch whether it holds in coming quarters.
insights.quote: They're getting sub 12-month payback periods, right? which is obviously a signal for demand.

insights.claim: Owning vertically integrated AI players (app, model and compute layers) is risk-adjusted because they benefit whether open-source or closed models win and can redirect capacity to their own products if external demand slows.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Prefer full-stack AI owners over single-layer bets to hedge model-mix and demand uncertainty.
insights.quote: if you're going to invest anywhere within this space, you probably want to own the vertically integrated players

insights.claim: Because SpaceX builds compute capacity fastest, its capex runs in shorter-duration cycles, letting it reach payback and pull back quickly if markets shift, lowering capex risk.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Build speed is a capex-risk mitigant; short cycles reduce stranded-asset risk versus slower builders.
insights.quote: And also if you build these things fast, you can pull back on these things really fast, right?

insights.claim: Over 50% of SpaceX revenue was reported as attributable to AI in some capacity, but Garrett expects the revenue mix to shift back as launch, Starlink and direct-to-cell grow on their own S-curves.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Don't anchor SpaceX comps solely to AI; segment mix will rotate as Starship and DDC scale.

insights.claim: Starship is working and underappreciated: a launch of just a handful of Starlink V3 satellites delivered roughly 1% of the world's capacity, and SpaceX plans to deploy tens of thousands of them.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Starlink V3 capacity step-change implies large connectivity supply growth; negative for competing satellite/telecom capacity providers.
insights.quote: that launch on just a handful of Starlink V3s delivered like 1% of the world's right capacity.

insights.claim: Starlink is compounding and moving faster into direct-to-cell (DDC), which Garrett highlights as a fast-growing line.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Direct-to-cell is a growth vector to watch; read-across to mobile carriers and D2C competitors.

insights.claim: Garrett argues Starship is likely underpriced because even without full reusability it is already a viable launch vehicle compared with every competitor, and full reusability will cut cost and raise cadence further.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Market may be discounting Starship until full reuse; current version already beats peers.
insights.quote: this is probably underpriced that like the next phase is just getting this thing to being fully reusable

insights.claim: Starship should drive launch costs down by an order of magnitude, likely producing a commensurate rise in the number of companies built on cheap launch, as Falcon 9 did for companies like Varda.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Second-order: cheap launch spawns new space businesses (in-space manufacturing, pharma, defense); look for the next Varda-type startups.
insights.quote: Starship will not just drive launch cost down order of magnitude which probably then will lead to an equal rise in the number of companies that can be built.

insights.claim: SpaceX has publicly targeted launching its first orbital compute satellites in the back half of next year and appears on track; with Google testing in orbit and Starcloud building, data centers in orbit are the 'clear solve' for terrestrial power constraints.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Orbital compute is becoming a real category gated by Starship economics; watch the H2 next-year milestone.
insights.quote: the clear solve is data centers in orbit.

insights.claim: Garrett thinks Elon Musk's forecasts are probably very aggressive but notes he has historically been right depending on timeline.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Haircut Elon timelines, not directional calls.

themes.theme: AI capital markets, debt financing and pricing uncertainty

insights.claim: Recent public and debt market volatility in AI reflects doubts about whether revenue can support spend commitments and whether builders have access to capital to match those commitments.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Credit access is the binding constraint for AI capacity buildout; monitor spreads and financing for leveraged builders.

insights.claim: Garrett finds it ironic that both the beneficiaries and the spenders of AI capex sold off simultaneously, which he says shows market structure matters more than logic in the short term.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Indiscriminate selloffs across both sides of AI capex can create mispricings.

insights.claim: Because AI capacity is mostly debt-financed, cost of capital is decisive; Garrett agrees with Elon that companies with lower cost of capital will absorb much of the available financing at better rates.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Lowest-cost-of-capital players (SpaceX, hyperscalers) gain share versus levered neoclouds.
insights.quote: Elon's 100% right that, you know, there are certain companies that have a huge advantage, right, and a lower cost of capital.

insights.claim: Pricing AI companies is extremely hard because steady-state market structure (model pricing, open vs closed mix, compute pricing, cost of capital, power access) is unknowable, and investors struggle to believe even two years of earnings.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Valuations rest on out-year earnings with low visibility; size positions accordingly.
insights.quote: It's hard to believe in the next two years, right, of earnings, right? Let alone the next 20.

insights.claim: 137 Ventures prefers AI companies at the harness and app layer with third-party structural positioning, such as Cognition and Hex, because customers in coding, security and analytics want to route across models rather than rely on one lab.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Model-agnostic app-layer companies may be more durable than lab-dependent wrappers.
insights.quote: You know not every company wants to be reliant on a lab for certain types of products definitely on security definitely on coding

insights.claim: Garrett expects open source to be a large percentage of AI models and deployment, as it is in software.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Open-source share pressures closed-model pricing; favors compute and full-stack owners.

insights.claim: Garrett calls OpenAI and Anthropic two of the most impressive businesses built in a generation and argues broad consumer diffusion (relatives using ChatGPT) shows AI is still early, with markets over-extrapolating both good and bad.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Use volatility to buy durable AI winners; diffusion still early.
insights.quote: like all things, markets overextrapulate the good and the bad.

themes.theme: Growth investing framework: duration and power law

insights.claim: Duration of compounding matters more than single-year growth: SpaceX compounded about 40% for 20 years, and even 9% over 30 years yields roughly 13x.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Underwrite how long growth lasts, not peak growth rate.
insights.quote: it's incredible how really duration is what matters the most

insights.claim: As minority shareholders who cannot control holding period, 137 Ventures only concentrates in businesses it wants to own for decades.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Concentration should be reserved for multi-decade compounders.

insights.claim: Garrett would rather pay a 25% premium for a quality asset that becomes a 5x than buy a poor asset at a 25% discount.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Price premiums for quality are acceptable in late-stage private markets.
insights.quote: you'd much rather own a quality asset that's a 5x and pay a 25% premium to buy it

insights.claim: Late-stage valuations (Cognition ~$48B, Ramp ~$60B, Anderoll ~$90B) reflect both real growth and too much capital chasing too few growth-stage companies.
insights.speaker: Molly O'Shea / Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Private marks are partially capital-flow driven; expect mispricing but power-law payoff.

insights.claim: Ramp is still underlevered: underpricing and under-monetizing products, with adjacent products not yet launched, so it has substantial runway as it consolidates the back-office finance stack.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Ramp has pricing power upside not yet captured; positive for its trajectory toward a $100B+ outcome.
insights.quote: they're still underlevered uh, on a lot of parts of the business, meaning they're underpricing on things.

insights.claim: The COVID-era fintech capital flood mostly produced dead companies, but power-law winners like Stripe, Revolut, Nubank and Ramp more than paid for it; Garrett expects the same in AI and aerospace/defense.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: In overfunded sectors, be in the power-law winners; LPs should ensure exposure to top outcomes.
insights.quote: So yes, things will be mispriced because there's too much capital chasing too few opportunities. The power law will probably pay for that amount of capital.

themes.theme: Return of the conglomerate and dual-use defense

insights.claim: Garrett's 'return of the conglomerate' thesis: unlike 1980s conglomerates, which lacked synergies and were hard to value, modern ones share a common tech operating platform and/or vertical integration (Apple, SpaceX).
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Multi-business companies with shared platforms may deserve premium, not conglomerate discount.
insights.quote: I have this like return of the conglomerate sort of thesis right now

insights.claim: Anderoll is a 'lowercase c' conglomerate whose shared Lattice software/AI backend means every marginal product sold raises the value of the others, which Garrett expects to make it by far the power-law outcome in defense.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Anduril's platform flywheel is the core bull case; multi-product defense firms should outperform single-product neoprimes.
insights.quote: every marginal product sold right makes the value of the other ones go up

insights.claim: Garrett argues the West needs 'capital C' dual-use conglomerates selling to both commercial and government markets; Palantir and SpaceX are currently the only examples, each with majority commercial revenue.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Dual-use firms with commercial scale can subsidize defense capacity; favor defense names with dominant commercial businesses.
insights.quote: I think Palunteer and SpaceX are the only examples of this

insights.claim: Chinese defense primes derive about 68% of revenue from the commercial sector, and China's shipbuilding dominance in defense stems from being the dominant commercial manufacturer.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Defense capacity follows commercial scale; Western defense industrial policy alone is insufficient.
insights.quote: Like 68% of the revenue comes from the commercial sector.

insights.claim: Industrial policy alone cannot fund the defense capacity the West needs; companies must be dominant commercially to maintain and throttle defense capacity economically.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Watch for commercial leaders crossing into defense (as in enterprise software and cybersecurity) rather than pure-play defense startups.

insights.claim: Anderoll's move into computer manufacturing is part of a broader trend of companies repatriating capacity for commercial reasons rather than relying on industrial policy.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Reshoring driven by private commercial opportunity, not only subsidies.

insights.claim: Garrett co-founded an aerospace and defense scale-up platform (transcribed as Onadrim) that acquires European critical-industry suppliers, deploys technology, and scales them toward pan-European champions as long-term holders.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: New buyer of European defense suppliers; signals a TransDigm/HEICO-style consolidation play in Europe.

insights.claim: Unlike the US, where primes, PE and roll-ups such as TransDigm, Teledyne and HEICO consolidated suppliers, Europe's fragmented defense supply chain was never consolidated because it was not a growth market.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Whitespace for a 'HEICO of Europe'; European supplier valuations may rerate as consolidation begins.
insights.quote: there was definitely no rollups or definitely not a haiko of Europe that was consolidating suppliers

insights.claim: With 4,000 drone companies in Europe, the neoprime layer is overfunded and crowded, while the supplier layer below (components, manufacturing, engines) is underappreciated.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Avoid crowded European drone/neoprime bets; look at tier-2/3 suppliers.
insights.quote: now there's 4,000 drone companies in Europe clearly that this is like this is overfunded right and too crowded.

insights.claim: Production, not contracts or spending, is the main defense bottleneck, driven by supplier inability to scale, unwillingness to take capex risk, and capacity that has left Europe and the US.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Supplier capacity is where value accrues in rearmament; track production throughput, not contract awards.
insights.quote: you've been seeing that production is the big bottleneck right now, and a lot of that's because of the supplier level

insights.claim: Onadrim targets dual-use suppliers with durable, low-churn revenue whose capacity solves a critical defense bottleneck, even if most revenue comes from aerospace or industrials.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Screening criteria for investable European suppliers.

insights.claim: Garrett says the platform will announce its first acquisitions and partnerships with leading prime-type companies soon.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Upcoming catalyst for European defense supply-chain M&A.

themes.theme: Technology into hard industries and tech-sector risks

insights.claim: AI is making integration into PLCs significantly faster, which has made Garrett much more bullish on deploying technology in industrial manufacturing beyond low-hanging fruit like automating paperwork.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Industrial AI/automation is moving from paperwork to machine control; watch industrial software vendors.

insights.claim: Applied Intuition is expanding from automotive software into vehicle electronics, consolidating processing units, controllers and wiring to cut vehicle cost structure and enable autonomy across OEMs, construction, mining and trucking.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Software-defined-vehicle architecture is a cost lever for OEMs.

insights.claim: General Matter is reinventing uranium enrichment by applying modern tooling such as sensors to capacity whose state-owned incumbents still use Cold War technology.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Domestic enrichment is a reindustrialization theme with tech-driven cost advantages.

insights.claim: Deploying software into an industrial business does not make it a technology business; the margin and business-quality impact varies.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Don't pay tech multiples for software-enabled industrials by default.
insights.quote: Just because you deploy software into a business doesn't necessarily make it a technology business

insights.claim: Garrett warns that political weaponization of tech companies (Tesla car burnings, Anthropic boycotts, break-up-big-tech campaigns) sets a dangerous precedent and will backfire.
insights.speaker: Christian Garrett
insights.so_what: Political/consumer backlash is an emerging risk factor for tech names tied to polarizing founders.
